raw_response:
*[Thinking as this farmer, in her voice]*

I'm 58 now, my back isn't what it used to be, but I know these fields. I've been working this land since I was in my twenties — before my children were born. My husband drives to town most days now for work, so it's mostly me and my younger son on the farm. Eight mu. That's what we have. I keep five mu in wheat and maize — plant them one after the other, same land — and three mu I've always done cotton. My neighbor Zhang across the road does all cotton but I don't like having just one thing. If cotton prices drop bad like they did three years ago, at least I still have grain to sell.

**For the wheat:** I'll sow in early October, right after the rains cool things down. I use seed I saved from last year's harvest — same variety I've been growing for maybe eight or nine years. It does fine here, the neighbors all use similar seed. Before I sow I have the tractor man come and plow the field, then I spread one bag of the black compound fertilizer per mu and work it in. After sowing I wait. In spring, around March or April, when the wheat starts to shoot up and I walk the fields — if it looks yellow or pale I put down another half a bag of urea. Last year it looked pale so I did the full half bag. I'll do the same this year unless it looks better. I flood the field four times: once before sowing to wet the soil deep, once in December for the winter, once in spring when it's growing fast, and once when the grains are forming. Four times is normal here. Costs money with the pump but if you skip the winter water and it freezes hard, you lose everything.

**For the maize:** the minute the wheat combine leaves the field in June I have to move fast. Sometimes it's only three or four days before I need to get the maize seeds in or the season is too short. My son borrowed our neighbor's small planter last year and we got it done in two and a half days. You can't save maize seed — I buy the hybrid bag every year from the county supply shop, costs more but the yield is much better. I put compound fertilizer in before planting, and then when the plants are about up to my knee — maybe late July — I walk between the rows and scatter urea. I try not to let it touch the leaves. Last summer was wet so I only irrigated once. If it gets very dry at pollination time I'll pump again, but usually summer rains help.

**For the cotton:** this is the hard work. I start getting the seedlings ready in April and transplant late April. Cotton takes more out of me every year — all the spraying, all the picking. I spray pesticide every two weeks or so through summer, checking the undersides of leaves for bugs. I put compound fertilizer in before planting and then top up with a bit of urea when the bolls are developing in August. I pick three times starting in September and going into October. My arms ache for two months. I've thought about giving up the cotton mu but if I switch that land to more wheat-maize I'd need to change my whole schedule and I'm not sure what I'd do with myself in summer. Cotton at least keeps me busy and the price last year was acceptable.

My biggest worry this year is the fertilizer cost. It has gone up again. I'll try to use a little less compound on the maize — I think I slightly over-applied last year and it didn't make much difference to the harvest.
